name: Fatima Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we don't sell or campaign. What you say is confidential. Can you tell me about a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Fatima Ziegler, twenty-seven, and I lead five accountants at Atlas Accounts. I have a master's and a chartered accountancy qualification, and my pay is about typical for the job. We prepare accounts and tax returns, mostly for freelancers with uneven earnings. I open the dashboard, review exceptions, and call clients when a tidy number hides a messy life.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like finding a pattern before a client gets a surprise tax bill. I use AI every day and usually try a new feature before the rest of the team, though I check its answers against source records. What wears me down is chasing six apps for one person's income. I rent alone, have about three months of expenses saved, and there are some similar firms nearby if I need another job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be surprised after all the trials we've run, but I can live with a smaller gain. The daily tool saves me from rewriting the same tax letter three times, even when I have to fix its numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my team to keep using the checks that work and drop the flashy ones. I'd tell freelance clients that a neat dashboard still needs somebody to explain why the tax bill moved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job looks secure in that world. I'm a twenty-seven-year-old team lead at Atlas Accounts, paid around the usual level, with a master's and a chartered qualification. I rent a flat alone and have about three months of expenses saved, so I can handle a slow month, though not forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep running our weekly return review and using the tested AI letter checks every day. This winter I'd put another hundred a month into savings, funded by fewer delivery meals. I'd show the team the three errors the tool made last week, so we keep our eyes on the source records.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about rent and work. I like a useful tool, and a plateau would let me make the small gains without chasing a new platform every Friday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does the tool still miss something?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A wedding photographer came in with income from six different apps and no idea what was taxable. The dashboard showed six green ticks, but one app had counted a refund as income. I caught it by asking what had actually been paid back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you save the extra hundred?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hundred is extra, beyond the transfer I already make. I'd set it automatically on payday and see whether the delivery-meal cut holds for two months. If it doesn't, I'll lower the transfer rather than use a credit card.

say: I would keep **working checks** and discard flashy features.
I would tell clients a **dashboard** still needs explanation.
think: My **three-month cushion** supports this steady accounting job even if a client pays late.
I would welcome small gains without constant **platform changes**.
do: Keep the **weekly review** and daily tested letter checks.
Show colleagues **three recent errors** from source records.
Save **one hundred extra** monthly by cutting delivery meals.
feel: I feel **calm** about work and rent.
S0.quote: The dashboard showed six green ticks, but one app had counted a refund as income.
fieldNote: Her **daily AI use** continues because she finds small gains worth keeping.
A **three-month cushion** and typical pay leave her calm under a limited change.

steps.text: Keep weekly tax-return review and tested daily AI checks
Save extra hundred monthly by reducing delivery meals

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can already see a version of this in our freelance accounts. A tool reads receipts, drafts replies and flags late invoices while the junior team checks what it guessed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the partners to publish accuracy and staffing figures together. To friends I'd say the point is to give people better advice for the same fee, not quietly remove the first job on the ladder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might be promoted to run a larger automated queue, but that is not security if the queue needs half as many staff. I lead five accountants; two mostly check routine entries, and those hours could disappear. My own income could shrink if client fees fall faster than new advisory work grows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd run a four-week trial on our freelancer accounts and keep a log of wrong expense categories. I'd teach the team to use the review screen and put the error rate beside the hours saved. I'd propose moving two juniors onto client calls for one day a week, if partners will keep their paid hours during the trial.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, despite being interested. I can steer a pilot, but I cannot promise five jobs from one spreadsheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who could move into client calls?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Soraya, the newest accountant, knows every odd travel expense our photographer clients claim. I'd pair her with a senior on calls, not leave her alone with an error queue. A client who hears a calm explanation might stay with us even if software is cheaper elsewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the partners refuse paid call time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the partners to sign off on the paid call day before the pilot starts. If they refuse, I'll still test accuracy, but I won't tell my team those client roles are real. I would bring the numbers to our monthly staff meeting.

say: I would publish **accuracy and staffing** results together.
I would argue for **junior client work**, not only faster queues.
think: Our five-person **team hours** may shrink as routine checks vanish from freelancer accounts.
Lower **client fees** could reach my own pay.
do: Run a **four-week trial** on freelancer accounts.
Teach the team the **review screen** and track errors.
Move two juniors to **paid client calls** if partners approve.
feel: I feel **anxious** about my team and income.
S1.quote: I cannot promise five jobs from one spreadsheet.
fieldNote: A **four-week pilot** reflects her comfort with early tools and measurement.
Her **client-call plan** depends on preserving paid hours, which the partners have not yet agreed.

steps.text: Trial AI review on freelancer accounts for four weeks
Teach five-person team the new error-review screen
Move two juniors onto paid client calls if partners approve

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years changes the arithmetic. The review screen I know today would become a complete accountant by 2028, and Atlas might not need my team at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell clients we need clear responsibility for bad tax advice, and tell government to fund transition pay. At work I'd ask for an actual headcount plan, not a cheerful talk about new opportunities.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect to lose this accounting job in the first year after 2028. Nearly all my work is thinking on a screen; robots arriving around 2031 won't delay that. Three months of savings gives me time to move, but nearby firms will face the same cheap system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the automatic investments this month and hold the three months of expenses as cash. I'd apply now for the open payments-operations role at the transit authority if the salary covers my rent. In the first year after 2028, if Atlas cuts me, I'd take wage support while searching for work outside tax preparation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, even though I have a plan. My rent depends on a transit authority vacancy that could close tomorrow and wage support that may never exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move in with family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mother would offer her spare room, but she lives two hours away and needs quiet after night shifts. I wouldn't move in while my rent account could still cover three months. I'd tell her early that I might need help, so it isn't a surprise call on the last day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What exactly changes in your budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd protect rent and food first. The investments are small, but pausing them gives me room to breathe. I would check the transit vacancy is funded before spending a weekend on the application.

say: I would demand **responsibility for bad advice** and transition pay.
I would request a real **staffing plan** from Atlas.
think: My **screen job** could end soon after 2028.
Three months of **cash** may not outlast a common shock.
do: Pause **monthly investments** and keep the cash reserve.
Apply for the **transit vacancy** if funded and rent-covering.
Claim **wage support** after a 2028 cut while seeking work outside tax.
feel: I feel **alarmed** despite a practical plan.
S2.quote: My rent depends on a transit authority vacancy that could close tomorrow and wage support that may never exist.
fieldNote: **Thinking AI** reaches her accounting work in 2028; the robot date is irrelevant to most tasks.
Her **cash reserve** buys limited time, and the transit application depends on a funded rent-covering post.

steps.text: Apply for funded transit payments role if pay covers rent
Claim transition wage support after a 2028 layoff

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough time to build something clients actually ask for. I'd still assume the standard return gets cheap by 2031, so I'd start learning outside the return itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Atlas to test tools openly with clients and staff. I'd also ask the professional body to set clear rules for who checks an automated answer, because a confident error is still an error.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could move into helping independent workers plan cash for uneven months. A human may still be useful when a freelancer has to choose between rent and tax, though I wouldn't bet my whole future on that. The robots around 2034 are later, but my screen role is exposed in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd enrol in the evening cash-flow advice course if Atlas pays its three-hundred fee and grants paid study time. I'd run a small client clinic on Fridays if the partners agree to keep my paid hours. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, if return work ends, I'd apply for a funded community finance adviser vacancy that covers my rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but busy in a useful way. Five years is enough to learn what clients will pay for rather than guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you test demand for the clinic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use six current freelance clients for the clinic, with their consent. If three come back for a second session, that tells me there is a need beyond tax forms. If nobody returns, I'd change course before spending more money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why insist on paid study hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The course itself isn't expensive, but the paid study hours matter more than the fee. I don't want a career change funded by late nights until I burn out. I'd put both conditions in one written request to the partners.

say: I would demand **open trials** with staff and clients.
I would seek clear **checking rules** for automated advice.
think: My **return work** is exposed by 2031, even though robots for hands-on jobs come later.
A **cash-flow clinic** might show demand for different advice.
do: Enrol in **cash-flow study** if Atlas pays and releases me.
Run a **six-client clinic** if paid hours continue.
Apply after 2031 for a **funded advice vacancy** if returns vanish and salary covers rent.
feel: I feel **anxious**, but able to test demand.
S3.quote: I don't want a career change funded by late nights until I burn out.
fieldNote: The **six-client test** lets her judge demand before committing to a new niche.
Firm-paid **study time** is her condition for learning without exhausting evenings and weakening her present job.

steps.text: Enrol in cash-flow course if Atlas funds fee and paid release
Run six-client cash-flow clinic if partners preserve paid hours
Apply for funded community finance vacancy after 2031 if pay covers rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade gives me time to see which services survive, and to build one of them. I'd be thirty-seven when full AGI arrives in 2036, which is a very different horizon from 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should share productivity gains with staff and clients, and judge new services by what people need. I'd keep asking for named accountability on an automated tax return, because a client needs somewhere to take a complaint.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The standard return will likely be mostly automated by 2036. I could have a small advice practice by then, serving people with irregular income, but I don't know whether they would pay enough. Robots around 2039 don't grant more time to my desk job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd begin this year with a paid Saturday cash-flow session for two freelancers, if both book and pay the fee. I'd keep one hundred monthly in savings rather than putting everything into that experiment. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2036, if Atlas no longer needs my return team, I'd expand the practice only if its booked revenue covers rent for six months; otherwise I'd apply for a funded advice job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, because a decade can disappear in experiments that never earn. Still, I have enough time to test demand and stop a weak idea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would the first paid session happen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't rent an office for two Saturday clients. I'd use a private room at the library that can be booked by the hour, and charge enough to cover it. If they don't pay, I have learned something cheaply.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you leave the firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Six months of rent is the line I'd use before leaving Atlas. I'd show my mother the booked invoices, not a follower count. If the numbers fall short, I'll keep working and apply only to advice roles with a real salary.

say: I would ask the partners for **shared gains** and named responsibility on every automated return.
I would judge new services by **paid need**.
think: Routine **returns** shrink by 2036, despite the years I have to prepare for that change.
An **advice practice** is possible only if clients pay enough.
do: Offer a **paid Saturday session** if two freelancers book.
Keep saving **one hundred monthly** during the test.
Expand after 2036 if **booked revenue** covers six months of rent; otherwise apply for a funded salaried advice vacancy.
feel: I feel **uneasy**, but able to test and stop weak ideas.
S4.quote: I wouldn't rent an office for two Saturday clients.
fieldNote: Her **low-cost trial** tests freelance demand without assuming that two interested clients can support a practice.
She will **expand after 2036** only with six months of rent covered by booked revenue.

steps.text: Hold paid Saturday cash-flow session if two freelancers book
Save one hundred monthly while testing client demand
Expand advice practice after 2036 if booked revenue covers six months rent
Apply for funded salaried advice vacancy after 2036 if practice revenue falls short

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. My desk job could go before a small advice service has paying clients, and three months of cash is a short runway. Clear transition pay, open staffing plans and funded vacancies outside tax work would help. A trial project is not a wage until somebody pays the invoice.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what clients can afford. Freelancers can need advice badly and still have nothing left after rent. If their money isn't there, I can't turn empathy into a sustainable practice, however good the software gets.

headlineQuote: A trial project is not a wage until somebody pays the invoice.

She tests **paid demand** for cash-flow advice before considering an independent practice.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her accounting job before a new service has paying clients.
